title: SteamPressClear
question: How does a steam press work?
hook: Two thousand watts into a thick metal plate, a strip of two metals that clicks it on and off, and a few drops of water that flash into steam. Take an iron apart in 3D, see why steam unlocks a crease, and meet the laundry's boiler press and the istri-wala's charcoal iron.

explainer.title: A hot plate, a thermostat and some water
explainer.text: A steam iron is a thick aluminium or steel soleplate with a heating element cast inside it, a bimetal thermostat under the dial, and a water tank whose drip valve lets drops fall into a steam chamber on the hot plate. At 2,000 W it draws about 8.7 A from a 230 V socket.

explainer.title: Steam unlocks the crease
explainer.text: Cotton and wool chains are held in a fold by hydrogen bonds. Water slips between the chains and heat lets them slide above their glass transition; the iron's weight presses them flat. As the cloth cools and dries, the bonds re-form and lock the flat shape in. Polyester needs only heat, but melts if it is too hot: hence the care label's one, two or three dots, up to 110, 150 and 200 °C.

explainer.title: The heat sums
explainer.text: The soleplate stores about 620 J per degree, so 2,000 W brings it to 200 °C in about a minute. A brass-on-invar strip curls about 2 mm as it warms and clicks the element off and on. Turning tap water into steam takes about 2,550 J a gram, so a 2,000 W iron has heat to spare for only about 40 g of steam a minute.

explainer.title: The laundry's boiler press
explainer.text: A small boiler at 4 bar holds water at about 152 °C. Its steam blasts out about 1.5 g a second, arrives hotter than 100 °C and dry, and the hot water stores enough heat to flash into about 100 g of steam per litre. A pressure switch, a gauge, a sight glass and a safety valve keep it in check, and a vacuum table pulls the steam through the cloth and then cools it in seconds.

explainer.title: The istri-wala's charcoal iron
explainer.text: Five kilograms of cast iron store about 2,300 J per degree, so the istri-wala's box iron stays hot between loads of charcoal; blowing on the coals gives them more air and more heat. Burning charcoal makes carbon monoxide, so it must never be used in a closed room.

explainer.title: Safe and lasting
explainer.text: A gram of steam condensing on skin gives about ten times the heat of a gram of boiling water. Never leave an iron face-down, switch off and unplug when you step away and before filling, use an earthed socket, and never tamper with the thermostat, thermal fuse or auto shut-off. Hard water leaves limescale that clogs the steam holes.

concepts.def: The flat metal bottom of an iron that touches the cloth, with the heating element cast into it.
A switch, here a bimetal strip, that turns the heater off when hot enough and on again as it cools.
Two metals bonded together that expand by different amounts, so the strip bends when heated.
The heat that turns water into steam without changing its temperature: about 2,257 J for each gram.
A weak pull between neighbouring molecules; in cotton and wool it holds the chains in shape.
The temperature above which a solid's long chains can slide, so it softens and can be reshaped.
Pressure above the air outside, the number on a boiler's pressure gauge.
A valve that opens by itself if a boiler's pressure climbs past its limit. It must never be tampered with.
A poisonous gas with no colour or smell, made whenever charcoal or other fuel burns.
